evidence_quotes.quote: A large factorial field experiment in Mumbai’s informal settlements reveals that a bureaucratic facilitation drive significantly improved citizens’ ability to access municipal water connections in policy-eligible settlements, but only when combined with a bottom-up political coordination campaign targeting elected officials.
Our experimental sample comprises 153 slum clusters, which were demarcated during a mapping exercise carried out before the baseline survey.

We present two sets of pre-registered analyses: the first set using our entire sample of 76 slums, and the second set using our “eligible lands” sample which excludes those slums (28 slums in total comprising 36 clusters) that were located on lands rendered ineligible for formalization by the existing policy and legal framework—i.e., forest, footpath, and saltpan lands.

Moreover, as shown in the marginal effects plot displayed in Figure 6, we find that T1 raises the likelihood of full formalization by a statistically significant 19 percentage points (p-value=0.001) when T2 is also assigned, an increase which amounts to a substantial 45% of the control mean.

Our qualitative work highlights the important role that politicians’ intervention played at the infrastructural stage, revealing that this stage required obtaining approvals—known as “No Objection Certificates (NOCs)”—from multiple authorities and agencies who have jurisdiction over the land.

country.comment: Study was conducted in informal settlements (slums) in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 12–13, Section 'The Mumbai Context'

effect_estimate.comment: Pre-registered intent-to-treat WLS estimates with randomization-block fixed effects show strong complementarity between bureaucratic assistance (T1) and political coordination (T2), restricted to settlements not legally barred by footpath, forest, or saltpan land exclusions.
effect_estimate.value: In the full sample including legally ineligible lands (N = 6,652 households across 76 slums / 152 clusters), neither bureaucratic assistance (T1) alone (beta = 0.02, SE = 0.03, one-sided p = 0.26, control mean = 0.43) nor the T1*T2 interaction (beta = 0.11, SE = 0.08, two-sided p = 0.19, control mean = 0.33) significantly increased verified municipal water connections ('full formalization') at the 5-year endline. In the pre-registered policy-eligible lands sample (N = 5,251 households across 48 slums / 116 clusters), T1 alone was not significant (beta = 0.04, SE = 0.03, one-sided p = 0.08, control mean = 0.54), nor was T2 alone, but the T1*T2 interaction was positive and statistically significant (beta = 0.22, SE = 0.10, two-sided p = 0.04, control mean = 0.42; covariate-adjusted beta = 0.20, SE = 0.08, p = 0.04): when combined with political coordination (T2 = 1), bureaucratic assistance (T1) increased the probability of receiving a verified BMC piped water connection by 19 percentage points (p = 0.001, ~45% of the control mean) and increased the 0–3 ordinal formalization scale by 0.39 points (p = 0.046). At the 1-year midline (eligible lands, N = 5,010), T1 alone increased formal application submission by 10 percentage points (beta = 0.10, SE = 0.03, p < 0.01, control mean = 0.21) and BMC engineer inspection visits by 4 percentage points (beta = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01, control mean = 0.06), with no effect on P-form approval (beta = 0.01, SE = 0.01, p = 0.27) or midline connections (beta = -0.02, SE = 0.02, p = 0.88). Exploratory heterogeneity shows the endline T1|T2=1 effect was concentrated in eligible settlements requiring multi-agency land No Objection Certificates (AME = 26 percentage points, p = 0.006, N = 3,865) and during the 2020–2022 pre-election period (T1*T2 = 0.16, SE = 0.07, p = 0.04).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Assigned 4 (Experimental evidence): multi-level factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial (appraised with RoB 2 cluster-RCT variant) that experimentally manipulates bureaucratic assistance (T1) and bottom-up political coordination (T2), measuring both intermediate petitioning milestones (application submission, engineer inspection, P-form) and verified municipal water connections across legal land-eligibility regimes.

mechanism_flags.comment: The trial directly tests NGO bureaucratic assistance (T1: group formation, proof-of-address documentation, plumber sign-off, online portal submission, RTI requests) and bottom-up political coordination/participation (T2: community mobilization, petitions, delegations to politicians/bureaucrats) across multi-step connection procedures (application, USD 7 fee and USD 36 meter/pipe cost, inspection, P-form, C-form, land-authority NOCs), multi-agency institutional fragmentation and bureaucratic/political discretion, multi-year pre-election delays, and legal eligibility boundaries shaped by slum tenure/post-2000 illegality, land ownership/property categories, and Bombay High Court judicial orders (2014 PIL mandate vs. 2005 forest/saltpan prohibitions).
